T1110.name: Brute Force
T1110.description: Adversaries may use brute force techniques to gain access to accounts when passwords are unknown or when password hashes are obtained.
investigation_steps: Identify the source IP(s) generating failed login attempts
Check if the account eventually authenticated successfully
Review geolocation and ASN of the source IP
Check for the same pattern against other accounts (password spraying)
Consider blocking the source IP and forcing a password reset

T1078.name: Valid Accounts
T1078.tactic: Defense Evasion, Persistence, Privilege Escalation, Initial Access
T1078.description: Adversaries may obtain and abuse credentials of existing accounts as a means of gaining initial access, persistence, privilege escalation, or defense evasion.
investigation_steps: Verify the login originated from an expected location/device
Cross-reference with the user's normal working pattern
Check for concurrent sessions from different geographies
Review any privilege escalation immediately following the logon

T1059.001.name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: PowerShell
T1059.001.description: Adversaries may abuse PowerShell commands and scripts for execution, often to download payloads, evade defenses, or perform discovery.
T1059.001.detection_source: Windows Security Event ID 4104 (Script Block Logging)
investigation_steps: Review the full script block content
Identify the parent process that spawned PowerShell
Check for encoded commands, download cradles, or execution policy bypass
Correlate with network connections initiated by the PowerShell process

T1087.name: Account Discovery
T1087.description: Adversaries may attempt to get a listing of accounts on a system or within an environment to inform follow-on behavior.
investigation_steps: Identify the process/account performing enumeration
Check for use of built-in tools (net user, Get-ADUser, dsquery)
Correlate with subsequent authentication attempts against discovered accounts

T1136.001.name: Create Account: Local Account
T1136.001.description: Adversaries may create a local account to maintain access to victim systems.
investigation_steps: Verify the account creation was authorized via change management
Check the creator's account and its normal privileges
Review immediate follow-on activity (group membership changes)
Check whether creation occurred outside business hours

T1098.name: Account Manipulation
T1098.description: Adversaries may manipulate accounts to maintain access to victim systems, such as adding accounts to high-privilege groups.
investigation_steps: Identify who performed the group membership change and their authorization
Determine the sensitivity of the target group
Check for a corresponding recent account creation event
Review the target account's subsequent activity for privilege abuse

T1069.name: Permission Groups Discovery
T1069.description: Adversaries may attempt to discover group and permission settings to understand which accounts exist and their permission levels.
investigation_steps: Identify the process/account enumerating group membership
Check for correlation with subsequent privilege escalation attempts

T1548.name: Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism
T1548.description: Adversaries may circumvent mechanisms designed to control elevated privileges to gain higher-level permissions.
investigation_steps: Determine whether elevated privileges were expected for this account/context
Review the process that requested elevation
Correlate with any new IP/device risk factors

T1204.name: User Execution
T1204.description: Adversaries may rely on a user taking an action, such as opening a malicious attachment leading to script execution, to gain execution.
T1204.detection_source: Windows Security Event ID 4688, Sysmon Event ID 1
investigation_steps: Review the parent-child process relationship
Identify the originating file or email if available
Check the command line arguments of the spawned process

T1621.name: Multi-Factor Authentication Request Generation
T1621.description: Adversaries may repeatedly send MFA push notifications hoping the user accepts one out of fatigue (MFA push bombing).
investigation_steps: Count MFA prompts in a short window for the account
Check if any prompt was eventually approved
Verify with the user whether they initiated the requests
